30-second summary

  • Problem: Linen moves between hotel departments, but its context (identity, quantity, owner, deadline) doesn't. Staff rebuild the story through calls, WhatsApp and paper registers.
  • Approach: Five role-based interviews and a contextual enquiry, then a six-feature concept and a hi-fi prototype for Housekeeping, Laundry and Front Office.
  • Validation: 28 role-runs across six flows exposed 16 issues. I redesigned around the four high-severity ones.

The Solution

Familiar workflow, connected around it

Nexlin wraps the physical workflow with information, status and responsibility. The navigation is universal (Home, Requests, Scan, Inventory, More), and each role gets its own Home.

Request→Collect→Verify→Handoff→Process→Exception→Return
  • Verified handoff: the count is checked at the moment responsibility changes, not reconstructed afterward.
  • Two-sided transfer: a handoff stays "awaiting" until Laundry accepts it.
  • Quick Replace: an urgent path for the guest-is-waiting moment.
  • Structured QC: partial passes and rework are supported.
  • Reconciliation: Sent, Received, then Closed.

Context & Problem

The breakdown isn't tracking. It's continuity.

Guest rooms are a hotel's core product, and a room can't be turned over without clean linen. When linen is late, short or mixed up, rooms stay pending and guests notice.

Tracking already exists in the Indian market: RFID, barcodes, laundry software and hotel task tools. Yet the people I interviewed still relied on paper registers, phone calls and WhatsApp groups. So I reframed the problem.

The physical flow and the information flow are not always the same.

When an item changes hands, its status, destination and responsibility often stay behind with a person, a note or a chat thread.

Design question: How might we improve backstage coordination so item context stays connected throughout the journey?

Role & Team

End to end, solo.

I owned this project from secondary research and fieldwork through synthesis, concept, UX and visual design, usability testing and redesign. It ran across five academic milestones (A1 to A5) over roughly a month.

Users & Research

Listening across every handoff

Primary users: Housekeeping, Laundry and Front Office. Secondary stakeholders: Management, F&B/Kitchen, pickers and drivers, external laundries and guests.

Secondary

Literature & competitors

Literature review, plus ALICE, hotelkit, Treckme, Hotelogix, POXO, Xform and Indian laundry providers.

Primary

5 role-based interviews

Front Office, Housekeeping, F&B, Management and Laundry.

Field

Contextual enquiry

Floor and laundry walkthrough at Royal Residency, a small hotel with outsourced laundry. I chose it because a five-star property was hard to access.

Synthesis

POEMS + task flows

POEMS analysis, sub-task flows and a persona.

What I heard and saw

Front Desk cannot know the item's status without contacting the relevant department.Front Office interview
  • Housekeeping tracks linen in a paper register, with pending needs in a personal notebook plus WhatsApp.
  • Laundry and Management both named sorting and identifying items as the biggest manual coordination point.
  • F&B named following up on pending items as their hardest manual task.
  • A guest laundry batch was mixed with housekeeping linen, delaying its return to guests.
  • At Royal Residency I saw no individual item tags. Workers identified mixed laundry by hotel logo, then phoned the other hotel to arrange an exchange.

Insights

Six patterns, one root cause

  1. Coordination is distributed. Registers, notes, WhatsApp, calls and software each hold part of the story.
  2. Pending is an active state. Shortages are noted, communicated and rechecked, but nobody owns them.
  3. Item and information separate. The textile moves while status and responsibility stay elsewhere.
  4. Handoffs are high-risk. Every transfer between people or organisations adds ambiguity.
  5. Exceptions reveal the system. Mix-ups, damage and urgent needs are where it breaks.
  6. Operating models differ. In-house and outsourced laundries have different touchpoints.
Tracking the physical item alone is not enough. The service depends on people reconnecting information themselves.

The competitor scan pointed the same way. Textile platforms (POXO, Xform) are strong on lifecycle visibility. Hotel platforms (ALICE, hotelkit, Treckme) are strong on task orchestration. The gap is the link between them, especially when the workflow breaks.

Design Process

From research to a testable system

1. Define the concept

I proposed six features and used an impact/effort matrix to build the continuity model first. Automation sits on top, because it depends on trustworthy context and ownership.

Textile Continuity Passport

Identity, quantity, destination, deadline, condition, owner and next action stay together.

Accountable Handoff

Send, receive, acknowledge, new owner.

Live Item Journey

Where the item is, who has it and what happens next.

Exception Recovery

What happened, who acts, recovery, verification.

Dynamic Context & Priority

Deadline or capacity changes reach the affected teams.

Recovery Agent

Detect, understand, recommend. A human approves every decision.

2. Map six task flows

Each flow had a goal, information needs, a breakpoint and a link back to interview or field evidence.

Create request→Collect & handoff→Receive & sort→Process & QC→Handle exception→Return & reconcile

3. Set design principles

  • Context before complexity.
  • Verification before handoff.
  • Status, not just data.
  • Exceptions are first-class.
  • Design for the shift: frequent actions are quick and low-friction.
  • Shortcuts don't replace universal navigation.

4. Design for real hotel tempo

Real operations aren't one logging sequence. When a guest is waiting, the room gets its linen first. So I added Quick Replace: replace now, reconcile later.

5. Build accessibility in

Status never relies on color alone. Touch targets are 44px or larger, text meets WCAG AA contrast, and the front-desk web view supports full keyboard navigation.

Prototype & Testing

Every flow passed. With issues.

I tested the hi-fi Figma prototype with four participants (Housekeeping ×2, Laundry, Front Desk) across six flows: 28 role-runs, 16 issues, 4 high severity. The four highest-risk findings:

FindingWhat a participant saidSeverity
Quick Replace had no visible entry on Home"Where's the quick one? I don't want to raise a whole request."High
"Record later" loop had no owner or reminder"Later, when I'm free… where do I find this again?"High
Handoff confirmed without the receiver"It says confirmed. Did Laundry actually accept it?"High
Quantity checks were ticks, not counts"Count's already ten, fine."High

Seven patterns sat behind these: symbolic verification, one-sided handoffs, a fragile urgent path, exceptions living beside the flow, status without owner or time, role-blind homes, and vocabulary drift.

Resolved, but I still don't have my sheets.Housekeeping and Front Desk participants. A decision was being read as a physical recovery.

What I changed

  • Quick Replace became the first action on Home.
  • Replace Now and Confirm & Go merged into one commit. Wording now says what happened ("Bedsheet replaced"), not "Room is ready".
  • Counts are typed in. A mismatch blocks Next and opens a prefilled report.
  • QC splits pass and rework, so eight good items aren't held up by two stained ones.
  • Laundry got its own Home, with due times and at-risk states.

Metrics & Impact

What I can show, and what I can't

I haven't measured the redesign in live operations, so I won't claim outcome numbers. What the evidence supports:

  • Research depth: 5 interviews, 1 contextual enquiry, 6 competitors benchmarked.
  • Testing rigor: 28 role-runs and 16 issues, each traced to a redesign decision.
  • Highest risks addressed: all four High issues have a redesigned answer in the Figma file.
  • Known gaps: the Receive, Sort & Identify step and all Front Desk screens weren't in the tested prototype.

The redesign hasn't been retested yet, so the impact so far is risk reduction, not proven performance gains.

Learnings & Next Steps

What this taught me

  • Tracking is a crowded space. The opportunity was in the connections between tools.
  • A green tick can hide a failure. Nobody counted, and testing exposed it fast.
  • Urgent and routine flows need different designs. One logging sequence fails the people who need speed most.
If a screen says "confirmed" but only one person has acted, it hasn't confirmed anything.

Next steps

  1. Design and test Receive, Sort & Identify, the highest-risk research step.
  2. Add a Front Desk view with room-based lookup, not just request-ID lookup.
  3. Retest the redesign, and add out-of-stock, mismatch, offline and overdue states.
  4. Pilot in a higher-volume hotel and measure follow-up calls, mix-ups and handoff time against a baseline.
